summary:
Colima is a state of Mexico, and a trans visitor's exposure there is set by the national framework rather than by any Colima statute identified in the sources reviewed. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised anywhere in the country, and nothing in the inventory indicates that Colima has enacted a law targeting trans presence.

Legal gender recognition in Mexico is decided state by state. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that, as of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operate one in practice without enactment, six legislatures have enacted none, and only seven states extend recognition to children. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. The sources reviewed do not state which of these categories Colima falls into, so a visitor should not assume a recognition procedure exists there.

Where no state procedure exists, the consequences are documented. Human Rights Watch records identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. A joint Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024, written from Tabasco, found that without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and excludes trans people from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. That report also records the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and notes that more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.

Transfemicide has been made a specific crime in two of Mexico's 32 states. Mexico City passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' in July 2024, punishable by up to 70 years, following Nayarit, which set a maximum of 60 years. Impunity for transfemicide is thought to run higher than the already high general homicide impunity rate. Colima has not been identified in the sources as having enacted such a statute.
tangentialFactors:
The national lethality picture sets the background level for any state, including Colima: more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished in 2022, and transfemicide impunity is thought to be higher still. Transfemicide has been criminalised as a distinct offence in only two of the country's 32 states, Nayarit and Mexico City, so in most states including Colima such a killing would be prosecuted, if at all, under ordinary homicide provisions.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires all member states to provide a simple, accessible legal gender recognition procedure, and Mexico's Supreme Court has issued binding guidelines to the states. These create a legal floor that Colima stands under even where local enactment is absent, though the sources do not document how Colima complies in practice.
localsOnly:
Residents of Colima, like residents of every Mexican state without an enacted recognition procedure, must rely on the Supreme Court's binding guidelines and the Inter-American framework rather than a local statute, if Colima is among the six states with no enacted procedure. The sources reviewed do not confirm Colima's status either way.

Trans residents of any Mexican state without a recognition procedure face the documented pattern recorded in Tabasco and Guanajuato: identity-document mismatch producing discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, and every document request or appearance scrutiny carrying a risk of violence, harassment and humiliation.
outOfScopeNotes:
Colima's own status on legal gender recognition is unresolved in the sources reviewed: the inventory gives national counts (22 states with an enacted procedure, two operating one in practice, six with none, seven extending recognition to children) but does not say which category Colima occupies. This should be verified against the HRW state-by-state breakdown before publication.

No Colima-specific enforcement data, hate-crime statistics, facility or bathroom rules, or documented incidents involving trans people in Colima appear in the inventory. Their absence is not evidence that such incidents or rules do not exist.

Whether Colima has enacted a transfemicide statute, or any trans-specific criminal penalty enhancement, is not sourced here; only Nayarit and Mexico City are documented as having done so.
